analysis.headline: The Senate Homeland Security Committee approved the bill in July 2024, reported it on December 19, 2024, and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban Members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and similar investments — diversified mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, and Treasury securities would remain allowed. Members would have to divest banned holdings or put them in a qualified blind trust by set deadlines, and ethics offices would enforce the rules with civil penalties, publish compliance certifications online, fine members $500 for each missed STOCK Act trade report, and put financial disclosures into a searchable electronic format. The version the committee approved went further than the original: it added the President, Vice President, and their families, added digital assets like crypto to the banned list, phased out future blind trusts, and set the main effective date at March 31, 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, in two ways. First, laws and oversight would be written by lawmakers who cannot hold — or trade on — stock in the companies they regulate, or in Treasury-sensitive assets while shaping fiscal policy. Second, voters get more transparency: certifications, trust documents, and penalties would be posted on public ethics-office websites, and financial disclosure reports would have to be filed electronically and searchable by filer, asset, ticker, and date. The House and Senate ethics offices also gain clear enforcement tools they currently lack for stock conflicts.

how_it_helps.text: Bans Members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children from purchasing or selling individual stocks, commodities, and futures, with exceptions only for diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, Treasury securities, and a short list of other holdings like municipal bonds and spouse employment compensation.

Requires members to divest banned holdings or place them in a qualified blind trust within 120 days of the effective date (with limited extensions), and imposes civil penalties equal to the greater of one month's pay or 10% of the value of each un-divested investment, repeating every 30 days while a member stays out of compliance.

Requires the House and Senate ethics offices to publish online each member's compliance certification, blind trust agreements, schedules of assets placed in trusts, and any penalties imposed — so the public can see who is complying.

Adds a $500 fine for every failure to file a required STOCK Act transaction report and requires financial disclosures to be filed electronically in a searchable, downloadable format with public API access.

The committee-approved substitute expanded coverage to the President, Vice President, and their spouses and dependent children, added digital assets to the banned investments, and barred covered officials from maintaining qualified blind trusts going forward (existing trusts must be liquidated and dissolved).

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress who own individual stocks are the concentrated losers: they would have to sell those holdings, move them into a blind trust (which the committee version then phases out), or accrue monthly penalties of a month's salary or 10% of the un-divested holdings' value. The committee version extended the same divestiture burden to the President and Vice President. Members with large or complicated family portfolios — including those holding stock through investment funds, holding companies, or deferred-compensation arrangements — bear the largest compliance cost. The cost is not primarily monetary; it is the loss of the ability to keep personal wealth invested in individual companies while writing the rules that affect those companies.

drawbacks.text: The carve-outs are wide enough that well-advised families keep routes in. Excluded from the ban: stock received as compensation from a spouse's employer or corporate board service, trading done by a spouse in the course of their primary occupation, small-business interests, investment-grade corporate bonds held at enactment, and Alaska Native Claims Settlement stock.

The committee version's main mandate does not start until March 31, 2027 — roughly two years after hypothetical enactment — so members serving terms that end before then would never be covered, and a future Congress could revisit it before it bites.

Forced divestment is a real burden and could trigger capital-gains taxes on appreciated stock; the bill mitigates this by extending the existing Section 1043 tax-deferral rule for conflict-of-interest sales to covered officials, but members with complex or illiquid holdings still face a genuine cost and administrative load.

A good-faith objection from opponents: the ban tells people what they may do with their own legally earned money and could deter financially successful candidates from running; the bill answers this only partially, since diversified index funds remain fully allowed while only concentrated, company-specific bets are barred.

Enforcement is entirely civil and rests on the House and Senate ethics offices to notice violations, issue notices, and collect penalties — the same offices whose past willingness to police member conduct is limited; there is no independent prosecutor for the divestment mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is sound: members keep diversified index funds and Treasuries, so no one is forced out of investing entirely — they only lose the ability to hold concentrated positions in individual companies they can influence, which is the conflict that matters. The honest weaknesses are the March 2027 delayed start, the family carve-outs, and civil-only enforcement through ethics offices, each of which narrows the bill's real-world effect. Even taken at full strength, the benefit is trust and cleaner lawmaking rather than a direct paycheck change for ordinary people, so it is a meaningful but indirect public gain weighed against a real cost that falls exclusively on the officeholders themselves.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Homeland Security committee reported the bill favorably and it was placed on the Senate's Legislative Calendar under General Orders, but no senator ever called it up and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on April 17, 2023 with 23 original cosponsors (21 Democrats and 2 independents); it was read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
The bill sat in committee for over a year before the committee ordered it reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 24, 2024.

On December 19, 2024, Senator Peters reported the bill from committee with a substitute amendment (Senate Report 118-309). The substitute expanded the ban to the President and Vice President, added digital assets, phased out qualified blind trusts, and delayed the main effective date to March 31, 2027.
The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 729) — the list of bills eligible for floor consideration — but no floor action followed.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the Senate never having debated or voted on the bill; no House action on a companion appears in the record.
Under Senate practice, bills die at the end of a Congress and must be reintroduced in the next one to move again.

The committee's action shows the substance was viable: a committee majority approved it favorably, twice, and it cleared to the floor calendar — it failed for lack of floor time, not for lack of committee support.
The bill drew no Republican cosponsors in the Senate, so the coalition behind it was Democrats and independents (23 of 100 senators) — not enough on its own to guarantee floor time or passage.

key_actors.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1171 on April 17, 2023 and recruited 23 original cosponsors; the bill carried his name through the committee process.

key_actors.name: Sen. Gary Peters
key_actors.role: Senator who reported the bill from the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
key_actors.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the full Senate on December 19, 2024 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute (Report 118-309), after the committee had ordered it reported favorably on July 24, 2024 — moving it to the Senate calendar in the final weeks of the Congress.

key_actors.name: Senate Majority Leader
key_actors.role: Controls which bills get Senate floor time
key_actors.what_they_did: Never brought S. 1171 to the floor for debate or a vote; the bill remained on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders from December 19, 2024 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

key_actors.name: Cosponsors of S. 1171
key_actors.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, including Sens. Brown, Gillibrand, King, Sanders, Tester, and Warren; no Republican senator cosponsored the bill.
